concepts.title: gradient arrays for backpropagation
concepts.one_liner: $g_l$ and $L$ represent arrays of partial derivatives key for backpropagation.
concepts.content:
Here we have introduced two new shorthands, $\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{g}$; these represent arrays of partial derivatives, defined below, and they are the key arrays we need to keep track of to do backprop. They are defined as:  

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_l&\triangleq \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_l} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{grad of cost with respect to } \mathbf{x}_l \quad [1 \times |\mathbf{x}_l|]\\
    \mathbf{L}&\triangleq \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \theta]} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{grad of layer}\\
    &\quad\quad \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} \triangleq \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{\quad with respect to layer input data} \quad [|\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}| \times |\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}|]\\
    &\quad\quad \mathbf{L}^{\theta} \triangleq \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial \theta} &&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{\quad with respect to layer params} \quad [|\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}| \times |\theta|]
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Tracking these gradient arrays is essential for performing backpropagation and updating parameters efficiently.
concepts.recap_md:
- $\mathbf{g}_l$ is the gradient of cost w.r.t. $\mathbf{x}_l$.
- $\mathbf{L}$ is the gradient of the layer output w.r.t. inputs and parameters.
- $\mathbf{L}^\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{L}^\theta$ specify gradients w.r.t. inputs and parameters respectively.

position.section_title: The Full Algorithm: Forward, Then Backward

concepts.one_liner: The full backpropagation algorithm consists of a forward pass through the network followed by a backward pass computing gradients for each layer.
concepts.content:
We can compute the gradient update for parameters $\theta_l$ once we have the arrays $\mathbf{L}_l$ and $\mathbf{g}_l$ for layer $l$. To ensure these arrays are ready when updating layer $l$, we first perform a forward pass through the entire network, starting with input data $\mathbf{x}_0$ and evaluating layer by layer to produce the sequence $\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$. (see figure: Forward pass.)

Data/activations passed forward through the network are shown in green.

Next, we compute a backward pass, iteratively evaluating the gradients $\mathbf{g}$ to obtain the sequence $\mathbf{g}_L, \mathbf{g}_{L-1}, \ldots$, as well as the parameter gradients for each layer. (see figure: A schematic diagram of the backpropagation process in a neural network. Red arrows flow from right to left, starting with a value of 1 entering a loss derivative block $\mathcal{L}'$, then passing...)

The full algorithm is summarized in algorithm @alg-backpropagation-backprop_for_chains.

concepts.title: Backpropagation Over Data Batches
concepts.one_liner: The gradient of a sum of terms is the sum of the gradients of each term.
concepts.content:
So far, we have only examined computing the gradient of the loss for a single datapoint $\mathbf{x}$. The total cost function we wish to minimize is typically the average of the losses over all datapoints in a training set $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. Once we know how to compute the gradient for a single datapoint, we can compute the gradient for the whole dataset using the identity:

$$\frac{\partial \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N J_i(\theta)}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\partial J_i(\theta)}{\partial \theta}$$

where $J_i(\theta)$ is the loss for a single datapoint $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$. Therefore, to compute a gradient update for algorithms like stochastic gradient descent, we apply backpropagation in batch mode by running it over each datapoint in the batch (which can be done in parallel) and then averaging the results.

In the remaining sections, we focus on backpropagation for the loss at a single datapoint, keeping in mind that batch backpropagation simply requires applying the above averaging.

- Gradient of the average loss equals the average of the gradients.
- Batch backpropagation applies backprop to each datapoint and averages results.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a Linear Layer
concepts.one_liner: Forward for a linear layer is $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$, and backward gradients can be computed using matrix multiplies involving $\mathbf{W}$ and the input/output gradients.
concepts.content:
A linear layer's forward operation is defined as:
$$\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$$
where $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ is $N$-dimensional, $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$ is $M$-dimensional, $\mathbf{W}$ is an $[M \times N]$ matrix, and $\mathbf{b}$ is an $M$-dimensional vector.

The gradients of this function with respect to inputs and parameters are:

$$\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{W} \quad [M \times N], \quad \mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{I} \quad [M \times M]$$

There is no simple shorthand for $\mathbf{L}^\mathbf{W}$, but the backward operation can be implemented by plugging these into the backpropagation equations:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} \mathbf{W} \\
    \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}} &= \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} \\
    \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{b}} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}
\end{aligned}$$

The gradient $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}}$ is an outer product between $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$. This avoids building a large sparse matrix for $\mathbf{L}^\mathbf{W}$.

(see figure: The forward and backward matrix multiples for a linear layer.)

(see figure: Matrix multiply for parameter gradient of a linear layer.)

(see figure: Linear layer forward and backward.)

All these operations mainly involve matrix multiplies and are straightforward to implement using any library that provides matrix multiplication (`matmul`).

- Backward pass gradients: $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} \mathbf{W}$, $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{W}} = \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$, $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$.
- The parameter gradient is an outer product of input activations and output gradients.

concepts.title: Backpropagation for a Pointwise Nonlinearity
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation for a pointwise nonlinearity involves multiplying the output gradient by a diagonal matrix of derivatives of the nonlinearity applied elementwise.
concepts.content:
Pointwise nonlinearities have simple backward functions. Let a scalar nonlinearity be $h: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with derivative $h^{\prime}: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. Define a pointwise layer as
$$f(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) = [h(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^\mathsf{T}$$

Then the Jacobian matrix is diagonal:
$$\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = f^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) = \texttt{diag}([h^{\prime}(x_{\texttt{in}}[0]), \ldots, h^{\prime}(x_{\texttt{in}}[N-1])]^{\mathsf{T}}) \triangleq \mathbf{H}^{\prime}$$

There are no parameters to update, so the backward operation computes:
$$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} \mathbf{H}^{\prime}$$

For example, for a ReLU layer:

concepts.title: Backpropagation for Loss Layers
concepts.one_liner: The backward pass for an $L_2$ loss layer computes the gradient as $2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})$, the per-dimension error between prediction and target.
concepts.content:
The loss layer for an $L_2$ loss function is defined as $\left\lVert \hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y} \right\rVert^2_2$, where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the network output and $\mathbf{y}$ is the ground truth.

This layer has no parameters, so we only derive the backward gradient:

$$\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}} = \frac{\partial \left\lVert \hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y} \right\rVert^2_2}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{y}}} = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) \quad [1 \times |\mathbf{y}|]$$

The backward gradient signal is:

$$\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}} = \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} * 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}) = 2(\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})$$

Here, $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial J} = 1$ since the output of the loss layer is the cost $J$.

Thus, the backward signal is a row vector of per-dimension errors between prediction and target.

(see figure: Matrix multiply for `backward` of an $L_2$ loss layer.)

concepts.title: Putting It All Together: Backpropagation through an MLP
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation through an MLP involves a forward pass computing activations and a backward pass computing gradients, with backward operations corresponding to transposed weight matrices and gating from nonlinearities.
concepts.content:
Consider an MLP with input $\mathbf{x}$ (4-dimensional), hidden layers $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{h}$ (3-dimensional each), and output $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ (2-dimensional). The forward pass computes activations layer by layer. (see figure: Forward pass through an MLP.)

For the backward pass, gradients $\mathbf{g}$ are treated as column vectors (transposed from the usual row vector convention). Using the matrix identity $(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^\mathsf{T} = \mathbf{B}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}$, the backward operation is:

$$\mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{in}} = (\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}} \mathbf{W})^\mathsf{T} = \mathbf{W}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$$

This shows that backward for a linear layer is the same as forward but with transposed weights (biases are ignored in backward to activations).

Nonlinearities like ReLU act as gating matrices in backward, masking gradients where activations were negative. All backward operations are matrix multiplies, regardless of the forward operation.

Parameter gradients at each backward step are outer products of input activations and output gradients. 

This unifies forward and backward passes as matrix operations within the network.

concepts.one_liner: The full backpropagation algorithm can be viewed as one big neural network combining the forward and backward passes.
concepts.content:
The backward pass through a neural network can itself be implemented as another neural network—a linear network with parameters determined by the original network's weights and activations. Therefore, the full backward pass is a neural network.

Since the forward pass is also a neural network (the original network), the full backpropagation algorithm—a forward pass followed by a backward pass—can be viewed as one big neural network.

Parameter gradients can be computed from this combined network via one additional matrix multiply (`matmul`) for each layer of the backward network.

position.section_title: Backpropagation through DAGs: Branch and Merge

concepts.one_liner: In a DAG, nodes can have multiple inputs and outputs, and backpropagation handles this using special 'merge' and 'branch' operators.
concepts.content:
So far we have only seen chain-like graphs, --\[\]--\[\]--\[\]$\rightarrow$. Can backprop handle other graphs? It turns out the answer is *yes*. Presently we will consider (**DAGs**). In @sec-recurrent_neural_nets, we will see that neural nets can also include cycles and still be trained with variants of backprop (e.g., backprop through time).

In a DAG, nodes can have multiple inputs and multiple outputs. In fact, we have already seen several examples of such nodes in the preceding sections. For example, a linear layer can be thought of as having two inputs, $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ and $\theta$, and one output $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$; or it can be thought of as having $N = |\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}| + |\theta|$ inputs and $M = |\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}|$ outputs, if we count up each dimension of the input and output vectors. So we have already seen DAG computation graphs.

However, to work with general DAGs, it helps to introduce two new special modules, which act to construct the topology of the graph. We will call these special operators `merge` and `branch` @fig-backpropagation-branch_and_merge.

(see figure: The `merge` and `branch` layers.)

We only consider binary branching and merging here, but branching and merging $N$ ways can be done analogously or by repeating these operators.

We define them mathematically as variable concatenation and copying, respectively: $$\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{merge}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b) &\triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b] \triangleq \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}\\
    \texttt{branch}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) &\triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}] \triangleq [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^b]
\end{aligned}$$ 

What if $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b$ are tensors, or other objects, with different shapes? Can we still concatenate them? The answer is yes. The shape of the data tensor has no impact on the math. We pick the shape just as a notational convenience; for example, it's natural to think about images as two-dimensional arrays.

Here, $\texttt{merge}$ takes two inputs and concatenates them. This results in a new multidimensional variable. The backward pass equation is trivial. To compute the gradient of the cost with respect to $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}$, that is, $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^a$, we have $$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^{a} &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}^a} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}} \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}\\
    &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\Big[\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}, \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{b}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}\Big]^\mathsf{T}\\
    &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}[1, 0]^\mathsf{T}
\end{aligned}$$ and likewise for $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^b$. That is, we just pick out the first half of the $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}$ gradient vector for $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^a$ and the second half for $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}^b$. There is really nothing new here. We already defined backpropagation for multidimensional variables above, and $\texttt{merge}$ is just an explicit way of constructing multidimensional variables.

The `branch` operator is only slightly more complicated. In branching, we send *copies* of the same output to multiple downstream nodes. Therefore, we have multiple gradients coming back to the $\texttt{branch}$ module, each from different downstream paths. So the inputs to this module on the backward pass are $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}, \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{b}}$, which we can write as the gradient vector $\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}= \frac{\partial J}{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^b]} = [\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{a}}, \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}^{b}}] = [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b]$. Let's compute the backward pass output: $$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{in}}&= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{L}^{\mathbf{x}}\\
    &= [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b] \frac{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}^b]}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}}\\
    &= [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b] \frac{\partial [\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}]}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}}\\
    &= [\mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a, \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b][1, 1]^\mathsf{T}\\
    &= \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^a + \mathbf{g}_{\texttt{out}}^b
\end{aligned}$$ So, branching just sums both the gradients passed backward to it.

Both $\texttt{merge}$ and $\texttt{branch}$ have no parameters, so there is no parameter gradient to define. Thus, we have fully specified the forward and backward behavior of these layers. The next diagrams summarize the behavior (@fig-backpropagation-branch_and_merge_layers_backprop_diagram).

(see figure: Merge and branch layers `forward` and `backward`.)

With `merge` and `branch`, we can construct any DAG computation graph by simply inserting these layers wherever we want a layer to have multiple inputs or multiple outputs. An example is given in @fig-backpropagation-backprop_DAG.

concepts.title: Backpropagation to the Data
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation treats parameters and data symmetrically, allowing optimization of data inputs as well as parameters.
concepts.content:
Backpropagation does not distinguish between parameters and data --- it treats both as generic inputs to parameterless modules. Therefore, we can use backprop to optimize data inputs to the graph just like we can use backprop to optimize parameter inputs to the graph.

To see this, it helps to think about just the inputs and outputs to the full computation graph. In the forward direction, the inputs are the data and parameter settings and the output is the loss. In the backward direction, the input is the number 1 and the outputs are the gradients of the loss with respect to the data and parameters. The full computation graph, for a learning problem using neural net $F = f_L \circ \cdots \circ f_1$ and loss function $\mathcal{L}$, is $\mathcal{L}(F(\mathbf{x}_0), \mathbf{y}, \theta) \triangleq J(\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{y}, \theta)$. This function can itself be thought of as a single computation block, with inputs and outputs as specified previously (@fig-backpropagation-J_forward_backward_blocks). 

In Pytorch you can only set *input* variables as optimization targets -- these are called the *leaves* of the computation graph since, on the backward pass, they have no children. All the other variables are completely determined by the values of the input variables — they are not *free* variables.

(see figure: Full forward and backward passes for a learning problem $\min J(\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{y},\theta)$, collapsed into a single computation block.)

From this diagram, it should be clear that data inputs and parameter inputs play symmetric roles. Just as we can optimize parameters to minimize the loss, by descending the parameter gradient given by `backward`, we can also optimize input data to minimize the loss by descending the data gradient.

This can be useful for lots of different applications. One example is visualizing the input image that most activates a given neuron we are probing in a neural net. To do this, we define $J$ to be the *negative* of the value of the neuron we are probing[^1], that is, $J(\mathbf{x}_0,\theta) = -x_{l}[i]$ if we are interested in the $i$-th neuron on layer $l$ (notice $\mathbf{y}$ is not used for this problem). We show an example of this in @fig-backpropagation-backprop_to_the_data_example below, where we used backprop to find the input image that most activates a node in the computation graph that scores whether or not an image is "a photo of a cat." Do you see cat-like stuff in the optimized image? What does this tell you about how the network is working?

(see figure: Visualizing the optimal image of a cat according to a particular neural net. The net we used is called Contrastive Language-Image Pre-Training (CLIP) @radford2021learning and here we found the image...)

Visualizations like this are a useful way to figure out what visual features a given neuron is sensitive to. Researchers often combine this visualization method with a natural image prior in order to find an image that not only strongly activates the neuron in question but also looks like a natural photograph (e.g., @olah2017feature).

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation is a general tool for efficiently finding partial derivatives in computation graphs, not just for training neural networks.
concepts.content: Backprop is often presented as a method just for training neural networks, but it is actually a much more general tool than that. Backprop is an efficient way to find partial derivatives in computation graphs. It is general to a large family of computation graphs and can be used not just for learning parameters but also for optimizing data.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: Deep nets transform data layer by layer into more abstract representations, effectively disentangling classes.
concepts.content: Layer by layer, deep nets transform data from its raw format to ever more abstracted and useful representations. It can be helpful to think about this process as a set of geometric transformations of a data distribution, or as a kind of disentangling where initially messy data gets reorganized so that different data classes become cleanly separated.
